title: PipeSDFA - RRAM-based IMC accelerator for SNN training via Direct Feedback Alignment
problem: Spiking neural network (SNN) training is computationally expensive, requiring efficient backpropagation alternatives. RRAM-based in-memory computing can provide efficient matrix operations but faces challenges with complex training algorithms.
motivation: Direct Feedback Alignment offers an alternative to backpropagation that requires fewer operations and can be efficiently implemented in analog RRAM-based in-memory computing without explicit weight matrices.
method: PipeSDFA trains spiking neural networks (SNNs—networks that operate through discrete pulses like biological neurons) using a specialized accelerator built from RRAM, a memory technology that performs arithmetic operations directly at the storage location. The forward pass (computing network outputs) uses analog multiply-accumulate circuits—this avoids the energy cost of moving data between memory and processor. For learning, it applies Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), a method that adjusts weights using direct feedback signals rather than computing gradients through every layer. RRAM's programmable resistance properties enable the hardware to implement both the forward computation and DFA weight updates efficiently.
key_novelty: This is the first system to train spiking neural networks on RRAM hardware using Direct Feedback Alignment, combining analog in-memory computation with a brain-inspired learning algorithm.
contributions: RRAM-based in-memory computing accelerator for SNN training
Demonstration of analog computing for neuromorphic learning
limitations: Direct Feedback Alignment may not converge as reliably as backpropagation for complex network architectures, and RRAM variability could impact training stability.
